ops.title: deployment: refuse to seal a daemonkit-linked binary carrying csflags-clearing entitlements
ops.description:
Follow-on from `3ea5b182` (codeidentity requires `CS_ENFORCEMENT|CS_HARD`). The runtime check is correct, but it can only ever fail *late* — at verify time, on a signed and shipped binary, with an opaque hex flag word.

**The measured latent wedge.** A full-machine csflags survey (1154 of 1157 live processes, `csops(2)`, cross-validated against the exact `SecCodeCopySigningInformation` path production calls) found all 7 daemonkit-linked first-party binaries carry both bits. But `ccx` — *same* signing identity (Developer ID Application: Yasyf Mohamedali, SXKCTF23Q2), same notarization path, same hardened runtime, and delivered through daemonkit's own artifact cache — measures `0x22010311`: `CS_ENFORCEMENT` clear, because it carries `com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory`.

Nothing is broken today only because `ccx` does not link daemonkit and is not a wire peer. The day any consumer that needs unsigned executable memory links daemonkit — an embedded Python, an ONNX/embeddings runtime, a WASM engine, precisely `ccx`'s shape — every keepalive verify against it fails at **runtime**, in production, with a flag word and no mention of the entitlement responsible.

**The fix: move the failure to seal time.** `deployment` owns sealed installation, activation, upgrade and removal of one fixed signed application. Its seal path should refuse a daemonkit-linked binary whose entitlements contain `com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory` or `com.apple.security.cs.disable-executable-page-protection`. The runtime check then only ever fires on tampering — which is what a runtime check should mean — and never on a mis-signed first-party build.

**Where the literals may live.** Not in `codeidentity`, and not anywhere a daemon-facing binary links: `TestDaemonFacingBinaryExcludesSignedOnlyPolicyLiterals` (`codeidentity/binary_absence_test.go`) forbids exactly these ten strings in such a binary, and it is load-bearing. A seal-time guard runs on the signing/CI side, so it can name them — but confirm the guard's package is not in any daemon-facing binary's import closure *and* not linker-reachable from one, since that test's real enforcement is dead-code elimination, not the import graph (see `c77fd33`).

**Related and NOT closed by this.** `com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit` and `com.apple.security.cs.allow-dyld-environment-variables` leave dynamic csflags bit-identical to a clean hardened-runtime binary — measured: Slack, Cursor, 1Password and Claude.app all carry `allow-jit` and sit at `0x22011311`, indistinguishable from clean. No status-word check can ever catch them; that needs the entitlement dictionary, which is `trust`'s lane. A seal-time guard could cover these too, and is arguably the only practical place to.

ops.text: deployment's seal path refuses a daemonkit-linked binary whose entitlements contain allow-unsigned-executable-memory or disable-executable-page-protection
The guard's entitlement literals are proven absent from every daemon-facing binary — verified by linker reachability, not by the import graph alone
A test pins the refusal with a fixture carrying each entitlement
The residual allow-jit / allow-dyld-environment-variables gap is either covered by the same guard or explicitly recorded as accepted
